changes.new: ### Pinned memory and a second stream: inspect the device timeline Vincent Moens profiles four combinations in [A guide on good usage of non_blocking and pin_memory() in PyTorch](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/intermediate/pinmem_nonblock.html). Each run transfers a CPU tensor to the GPU and multiplies an existing GPU tensor, `t3_cuda`, by itself twice. The multiplication does not read the transferred input. The operations may therefore overlap without violating a data dependency. A kernel that consumes that input would have to wait for its copy. The four original traces below distinguish two questions: when the CPU can continue submitting work, and whether the copy and kernel actually occupy overlapping intervals on the GPU. Their horizontal scales differ, so the widths of bars in different screenshots are not a speedup comparison. The stream numbers identify queues in the author's run, not dedicated hardware copy engines. Open a figure to enlarge its labels. With pageable CPU memory and both operations on the same stream, the device copy finishes before the multiplication starts. A host API call can return before device work completes without removing that ordering. ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/gpu-copy-2026-11-04/trace_streamed0_pinned0.png|PyTorch profiler: pageable input and one stream, with the H2D copy preceding the multiplication]] *Vincent Moens, [non_blocking and pin_memory()](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/intermediate/pinmem_nonblock.html), [original PNG](https://github.com/pytorch/tutorials/blob/5672cd98a7671eda4d9122b10f8eec580f74d03e/_static/img/pinmem/trace_streamed0_pinned0.png), [BSD 3-Clause, full notice](/licenses/pytorch-tutorials-5672cd98-BSD-3-Clause.txt). Complete source screenshot, unchanged. The copy and GPU kernel are consecutive; these are the author's measurements, not a Bookvar benchmark.* Pinning the source removes the need for a pageable staging path, but does not change the stream's order. In the second trace the source is pinned and the operations still run consecutively. ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/gpu-copy-2026-11-04/trace_streamed0_pinned1.png|PyTorch profiler: pinned input on the same stream, with no overlap between the H2D copy and multiplication]] *Vincent Moens, [non_blocking and pin_memory()](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/intermediate/pinmem_nonblock.html), [original PNG](https://github.com/pytorch/tutorials/blob/5672cd98a7671eda4d9122b10f8eec580f74d03e/_static/img/pinmem/trace_streamed0_pinned1.png), [BSD 3-Clause, full notice](/licenses/pytorch-tutorials-5672cd98-BSD-3-Clause.txt). Complete source screenshot, unchanged. Pinned memory alone does not make operations in one stream concurrent.* In the third trace the copy uses a separate stream, but the CPU tensor is pageable. The author's run still shows no overlap. Such a transfer can require staging through page-locked memory and can block the host during preparation. Creating another queue does not by itself provide a suitable source buffer or guarantee concurrent device execution. ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/gpu-copy-2026-11-04/trace_streamed1_pinned0.png|PyTorch profiler: pageable input with a separate copy stream, still without device overlap in the author's run]] *Vincent Moens, [non_blocking and pin_memory()](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/intermediate/pinmem_nonblock.html), [original PNG](https://github.com/pytorch/tutorials/blob/5672cd98a7671eda4d9122b10f8eec580f74d03e/_static/img/pinmem/trace_streamed1_pinned0.png), [BSD 3-Clause, full notice](/licenses/pytorch-tutorials-5672cd98-BSD-3-Clause.txt). Complete source screenshot, unchanged. The visible intervals belong to this pageable-memory experiment; they are not a portable transfer-time bound.* The fourth run combines pinned CPU memory, a separate copy stream and non-blocking submission. On the two GPU rows, the H2D interval intersects the multiplication interval. The hardware in this experiment can execute both at once. A busy copy engine, shared bandwidth or other work could reduce or eliminate the overlap on another workload. ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/gpu-copy-2026-11-04/trace_streamed1_pinned1.png|PyTorch profiler: pinned input on a separate stream, with overlapping H2D copy and independent multiplication intervals]] *Vincent Moens, [non_blocking and pin_memory()](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/intermediate/pinmem_nonblock.html), [original PNG](https://github.com/pytorch/tutorials/blob/5672cd98a7671eda4d9122b10f8eec580f74d03e/_static/img/pinmem/trace_streamed1_pinned1.png), [BSD 3-Clause, full notice](/licenses/pytorch-tutorials-5672cd98-BSD-3-Clause.txt). Complete source screenshot, unchanged. Compare the copy and kernel rows within this screenshot, rather than bar lengths across the four figures.* The profiling function waits for completion before returning. A CPU event-synchronization bar therefore appears even in the overlapping run. That wait finishes outstanding device work; it does not mean the copy and kernel were serialized before the wait. Pinning also has a preparation cost. Calling `pageable.pin_memory().to("cuda", non_blocking=True)` first allocates pinned storage and copies the CPU values into it. For a one-off transfer, that extra work can exceed the transfer time saved. Preparing reusable pinned buffers or using a DataLoader's pinning path moves that cost elsewhere in the pipeline; it must still be included in end-to-end measurements. The tutorial measures pinning, transfer and their combination separately. Its numerical timings describe the author's machine. ### Data readiness, allocation lifetime and source mutation The [PyTorch CUDA streams documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/notes/cuda.html#cuda-streams) states: > Operations inside each stream are serialized in the order they are created. Across streams, a consumer needs an explicit dependency on its producer. The corrected example in the documentation fills `A` on the default stream and sums it on a side stream. The source statements are retained below inside a CUDA-availability guard; a final synchronization makes the example wait before exiting. ```python import torch cuda_stream_example_executed = False if torch.cuda.is_available(): cuda = torch.device('cuda') s = torch.cuda.Stream() A = torch.empty((100, 100), device=cuda).normal_(0.0, 1.0) s.wait_stream(torch.cuda.default_stream(cuda)) with torch.cuda.stream(s): B = torch.sum(A) A.record_stream(s) s.synchronize() cuda_stream_example_executed = True print("CUDA stream example executed:", cuda_stream_example_executed) ``` *PyTorch contributors, [CUDA semantics, corrected side-stream example](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/5c4886908584029761b579af026dcfb627c84070/docs/source/notes/cuda.md#cuda-streams), [full source license](/licenses/pytorch-v2.14.1-LICENSE.txt). The wrapper and final wait are Bookvar additions. With no CUDA device, the example skips the device operations; that branch does not test a GPU.* `wait_stream` makes subsequently submitted work on `s` wait for work already submitted to the default stream. It enqueues a device dependency rather than blocking the CPU until `normal_` finishes. Consequently, `sum(A)` sees initialized values even if the CPU submits it early. A host read of `B` would also have to wait for the sum. `record_stream(s)` serves a different purpose. It informs PyTorch's caching allocator that `A`'s storage is in use on `s`, so that storage cannot be recycled for another tensor while the sum still reads it. It does not order the sum after initialization. Keeping a Python name alive, recording a stream and waiting for a producer address different parts of the storage and execution problem. The documentation also shows why a new `torch.empty` allocation can need a stream wait even when its old contents will not be read. The allocator may return storage previously used by pending operations on the allocation stream. Writing the new tensor on another stream without the dependency could collide with that earlier use. Pinned memory has another constraint: its contents can still be modified. Pinning prevents the operating system from paging out those pages; it does not prevent Python or another CPU thread from overwriting them. A non-blocking H2D copy may still be reading the source after the call returns. Likewise, after an asynchronous D2H copy, the CPU must wait before reading the destination. The tutorial's [other copy directions and mutation experiments](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/intermediate/pinmem_nonblock.html#other-copy-directions-gpu-cpu-cpu-mps) demonstrate these failures. In the earlier 3 ms copy and 7 ms kernel example, the pinned host source is no longer needed at 3 ms, when its H2D copy completes. The device input is still needed until the kernel finishes at 10 ms. The two buffers therefore have different safe reuse points: | Storage | Last reader | Reuse after | |---|---|---| | Pinned CPU input | H2D copy | 3 ms | | GPU input | Kernel | 10 ms | The following CPU model makes an early overwrite visible. It divides each read into two halves so that an overwrite can occur between them. This is a teaching interleaving, not a statement about actual DMA transaction size or the granularity of GPU instructions. ```python def read_interleaving(order): host = [1, 2, 3, 4] device = [None] * 4 seen = [None] * 4 for operation in order: if operation == "copy_left": device[:2] = host[:2] elif operation == "copy_right": device[2:] = host[2:] elif operation == "read_left": seen[:2] = device[:2] elif operation == "read_right": seen[2:] = device[2:] elif operation == "reuse_host": host[:] = [0] * 4 elif operation == "reuse_device": device[:] = [0] * 4 else: raise ValueError(operation) return seen safe = ["copy_left", "copy_right", "reuse_host", "read_left", "read_right", "reuse_device"] early_host = ["copy_left", "reuse_host", "copy_right", "read_left", "read_right", "reuse_device"] early_device = ["copy_left", "copy_right", "read_left", "reuse_device", "read_right", "reuse_host"] assert read_interleaving(safe) == [1, 2, 3, 4] assert read_interleaving(early_host) == [1, 2, 0, 0] assert read_interleaving(early_device) == [1, 2, 0, 0] ``` In `early_host`, the first half reaches the device before the overwrite; the second half copies the new zeros. In `early_device`, the copy finishes correctly, but the kernel's second read sees the overwritten device input. Both runs return a mixture of values. Waiting only for H2D completion prevents the first failure and still permits the second. A reusable input pipeline must keep the host source unchanged until its copy completes, delay the consumer until its device input is ready, and delay the next device write until the previous consumer finishes. Separate events can express these three dependencies without a global device synchronization at every step.
